title: I Will Go Down with You into Egypt — Sacrifice, Vision, a List of Names
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Let me open today with a question that is entirely practical: before you make a big decision, what is usually the first thing you do?
Run the numbers? Ask a friend? Look it up online? Weigh the advantages against the disadvantages? All of those are good. All of them should be done.

In Genesis chapter 46, Jacob is about to go down to Egypt. And this time every condition points the same way — go. His son is alive. Pharaoh himself has issued the invitation. The wagons are already standing at the door. The whole household is sitting in a famine, waiting for something to eat.
He has a hundred reasons to set out at once. And yet he takes a detour first. He goes down to Beersheba, and there he offers sacrifices.
1. He Went Round by Beersheba First
"Israel traveled with all that he had, and came to Beersheba, and offered sacrifices to the God of his father, Isaac." (Genesis 46:1)
Beersheba is not on the way. Travelling from Hebron down towards Egypt, Beersheba is a detour to the south. He went out of his way to get there.

Why Beersheba? Because that is where his family's altar stood. Abraham planted a tamarisk tree there and called on the name of Yahweh; Isaac built an altar there; and Jacob himself, fleeing for his life twenty-two years earlier, set out from Beersheba.
"Beersheba" (בְּאֵר שָׁבַע, *Be'er Sheva*) means "the well of the oath", or "the well of seven". It is a place where a covenant was sworn.
He is about to take a large step, and the first thing he does is go back to the place of the covenant.
And there is one very concrete worry on his mind. In Genesis 26:2, God had said to his father Isaac in the plainest possible words: "Don't go down into Egypt. Live in the land I will tell you about."
God had once plainly stopped his father from going down to Egypt. So Jacob does not dare to settle this on his own.

Brothers and sisters, this is an important lesson. When every condition points to the same answer, that is precisely when a person is least likely to pray — because it feels as though there is nothing left to ask.
But the conditions being right is not the same as the time being right. Having reasons enough is not the same as having God's permission.
And I want to press one thing deeper still: real asking means being willing to accept a no.

A great deal of the time we say, "Let me pray about it," when in fact our minds are already made up, and what we are after is a spiritual-sounding way of putting it. That is not asking. That is looking for an endorsement.
Here is the definition of asking: if God says no, I do not go. If you are not willing to accept a no, then you were never actually asking.
"God spoke to Israel in the visions of the night, and said, 'Jacob, Jacob!' He said, 'Here I am.'" (Genesis 46:2)
"Here I am" is הִנֵּנִי (*hineni*) in Hebrew — Abraham said it on Mount Moriah, Moses said it before the flame in the bush, Samuel said it in the night.
This is the last time in the whole life of this old man that Scripture records him hearing God speak to him directly. And his answer is those three words.
Notice one detail in passing. All through this chapter the text calls him "Israel" one moment and "Jacob" the next. And when God calls him, what God uses is "Jacob, Jacob!" — the old name.
God never pretends your old condition does not exist simply because he is giving you a new identity. He can name you exactly as you really are.
Every condition pointed to "go" — so why go round by Beersheba first?

Because the conditions being right is not the same as the time being right, and having reasons enough is not the same as having God's permission. And there was one very concrete worry on his mind: in Genesis 26 God had said to his father Isaac in the plainest possible words — "Don't go down into Egypt." God had once plainly stopped his father, so Jacob did not dare to settle it on his own. This is an important lesson. When every condition points to the same answer, that is precisely when a person is least likely to pray, because it feels as though there is nothing left to ask. And Beersheba was not on the way; it was a detour to the south — he was about to take a large step, so he deliberately went back first to the place where his family had sworn its covenant.
2. A Light from the Original: I Am Going Down Too, and I Will Surely Bring You Up Again
God says four things, and each one lands heavier than the last:

"I am God, the God of your father. Don't be afraid to go down into Egypt, for there I will make of you a great nation. I will go down with you into Egypt. I will also surely bring you up again. Joseph's hand will close your eyes." (Genesis 46:3–4)

The first thing: "I am God, the God of your father." He reconnects that line before anything else. The old man had offered sacrifices at Beersheba to "the God of his father, Isaac", and God answers him in precisely that identity.
The second thing: "Don't be afraid." In Hebrew, אַל־תִּירָא (*al-tira*). It is the sentence God speaks to human beings more often than any other in the Bible.

The third thing, and the most moving of them all: "I will go down with you into Egypt." In Hebrew, אָנֹכִי אֵרֵד עִמְּךָ (*anochi ered imcha*) — and that "I" is the emphatic form: I, I myself, will go down with you.
Brothers and sisters, please stop on that sentence.

What did Egypt mean to this family? It was the trouble Abraham brought on himself when he went down there. It was the place Joseph had been sold into. It was a foreign country with no altar in it and idols everywhere.
And God says: I am going too.
God is not standing at the border of the promised land, waving and calling out, "Off you go — you can do it." He says: I am going down there with you.
This is exactly what that later name means — Immanuel, God with us. He does not send us in; he comes in with us.
The fourth thing: "I will also surely bring you up again." The Hebrew, אַעַלְךָ גַם־עָלֹה (*a'alcha gam-aloh*), is the infinitive absolute — "I will surely, surely bring you up."

That sentence is the first seed of the entire book of Exodus. Four hundred years later, the God whom Moses heard as he stood before the burning bush would say, "I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians" — and in truth he had already said it on this night.
Brothers and sisters, when God said "go down", in the very same sentence he had already said, "I will surely bring you up again."

If you are walking a stretch of road right now that only goes downwards — income going down, health going down, reputation going down, spirits going down — please remember that God very rarely says only half of it. When he says "down", the day of coming up is already in his heart.

And the last line of the four is for an old father: "Joseph's hand will close your eyes." The Hebrew says literally, "he will lay his hand upon your eyes" — in the ancient world it was the nearest of kin who closed a dead man's eyes.
God said even a thing as small as that. He knows what a man of a hundred and thirty cannot get off his mind.
Then verse 5: "Jacob rose up from Beersheba." The Hebrew is וַיָּקָם (*vayaqom*) — "and he got up".

And verse 5 says they travelled "in the wagons which Pharaoh had sent to carry him". Those wagons revived his spirit back in chapter 45; in this chapter they carry him along the road. The tokens God gives us very often begin as a comfort and later become a tool.
An old man who had been saying for twenty-two years, "For I will go down to Sheol to my son, mourning" — that old man got up.
God called him with "Jacob, Jacob!" — why not the new name?

All through this chapter the text calls him "Israel" one moment and "Jacob" the next, and when God calls, what God uses is the old name. There is something very warm in that: God never pretends your old condition does not exist simply because he is giving you a new identity — he can name you exactly as you really are. And the man's answer is "Here I am" — Abraham said it on Mount Moriah, Moses said it before the flame in the bush, Samuel said it in the night. This is the last time Scripture records this old man hearing God speak to him directly, and he could still answer with those three words. To be able to answer like that at the last call of a whole lifetime is already a very good thing.
"I will go down with you into Egypt" — why does that sentence carry so much weight?

Think first about what Egypt meant to this family: it was where Abraham went down and brought trouble on himself, it was where Joseph had been sold, it was a foreign country with no altar in it and idols everywhere. And God says: I am going too. In Hebrew that "I" is the emphatic form — I, I myself, will go down with you. God is not standing at the border of the promised land, waving and calling out, "Off you go — you can do it." He says, I am going down there with you. This is exactly what that later name means — Immanuel. He does not send us in; he comes in with us. If you are about to walk into a situation you badly do not want to enter, that sentence is for you.
God said "go down" — so why does the same sentence add "I will surely bring you up again"?

"I will also surely bring you up again" is the infinitive absolute in Hebrew — "I will surely, surely bring you up." That sentence is the first seed of the entire book of Exodus: four hundred years later, when Moses stood before the burning bush and heard, "I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians," it had in truth already been spoken on this night. So God very rarely says only half of it: when he says "down", the day of coming up is already in his heart. If you are walking a stretch of road that only goes downwards — income going down, health going down, reputation going down, spirits going down — please remember that the second half of that sentence has not finished being spoken, and the one who is speaking it does not forget.
What comes next is twenty verses in which the text counts out names, one at a time.
A great many people start skipping at this point. But there are several things in this list that are worth looking at slowly.

First, the section opens like this: "These are the names of the children of Israel, who came into Egypt." "Names" in Hebrew is שְׁמוֹת (*shemot*) — and שְׁמוֹת is the Hebrew title of the book of Exodus.
In other words, the first sentence of Exodus picks up directly from this list. This is not a household register. This is where a nation begins.
Reuben is still set at the head of it and is called "Jacob's firstborn" — even though he had already forfeited the standing of the firstborn.
Among Simeon's sons there is one called "Shaul the son of a Canaanite woman" — the only grandson in the whole list whose parentage is specially noted.
Judah's branch reads: "Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah; but Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan." The names remain; the men themselves are gone.
And Perez — the child born out of that most sordid story in chapter 38 — stands here on the list, perfectly in order, and the line runs on from him to David, and on to Christ.
Third, the women are counted too. Dinah is named. Serah, Asher's daughter, is named. In a genealogy of that period, that is a very rare thing.
Fourth, that total: "All the souls of the house of Jacob, who came into Egypt, were seventy."

Brothers and sisters, please read that number alongside God's promise. God said to Abraham, "I will multiply your offspring greatly … like the sand which is on the seashore." God said to Jacob, "Your offspring will be as the dust of the earth."
At this moment the sand on the seashore is seventy people, riding in wagons Pharaoh sent, going down into Egypt.
The text offers no excuse for it, and it does not make the figure sound one bit larger. It simply writes it down honestly: seventy.
And four hundred years later, at the exodus, there were "about six hundred thousand on foot who were men".

So if the number of people you serve today is only seven, or only three; if your small group simply will not grow; if what you do feels so small that it is not worth mentioning — please remember that seventy.
God begins a nation with one household. When you set out to establish God's system, do not lose heart because there are only seventy people in front of you.

And I want to point out one more thing. Among these seventy there is a firstborn who failed, there are sons who died in their immorality, there is a daughter who was violated, there is a child born out of the most sordid story of all, and there are two grandsons borne by the daughter of an Egyptian priest.
God's list has never been a roll of honour. The people he took down into Egypt were exactly this sort of people.

There is one more word to notice. The unit the text counts in is נֶפֶשׁ (*nephesh*) — not "head of population" but "a living thing", a life. Of the branch Zilpah bore, the text says they were "even sixteen souls".

God is not counting heads; he is counting lives. He is not compiling statistics; he is calling a roll. When you feel that inside a large crowd you are nothing but a number, remember that word: with him you are a life, and you have a name.
Why is that list of seventy names worth reading slowly?

For several reasons. First, the word "names" at the head of it is in Hebrew the very title of the book of Exodus — the first sentence of Exodus picks up directly from this list. Second, the list is honest: Reuben is still set at the head of it and called the firstborn, even though he had forfeited that standing; Simeon's branch specially notes "the son of a Canaanite woman"; Judah's branch reads "but Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan"; and Perez, the child born out of that most sordid story in chapter 38, stands there on the list perfectly in order, and the line runs on from him to David and on to Christ. God's list has never been a roll of honour.
Only seventy people — is that number not far too small?

Please read it alongside the promise. God said to Abraham, "I will multiply your offspring greatly … like the sand which is on the seashore," and at this moment the sand on the seashore is seventy people, riding in the wagons Pharaoh sent, going down into Egypt. The text offers no excuse for it and does not make the figure sound one bit larger; it simply writes it down honestly: seventy. Four hundred years later, at the exodus, there were "about six hundred thousand on foot who were men". So if the number of people you serve is only seven, or only three, and your small group simply will not grow, please remember that seventy. And there is one more word to notice: the unit the text counts in is "a life", not "head of population" — God is not counting heads; he is counting lives.
"Jacob sent Judah before him to Joseph, to show the way before him to Goshen." (Genesis 46:28)

In chapter 37 he proposed selling his brother; in chapter 38 he learned to admit he was wrong; in chapter 43 he stood surety for Benjamin; in chapter 44 he begged to be made a slave in his brother's place; and in chapter 46 his father sends him ahead to lead the way.
Reuben is the firstborn. Simeon and Levi are older. And yet the one the father sends is Judah.
Brothers and sisters, a person's place is something he walks into one step at a time. Three chapters ago he was still the least likely candidate of them all.
"Joseph prepared his chariot, and went up to meet Israel, his father, in Goshen. He presented himself to him, and fell on his neck, and wept on his neck a good while." (Genesis 46:29)
"Fell on his neck" — when Esau embraced Jacob in chapter 33, and when Joseph embraced Benjamin in chapter 45, the text used this very same phrase.
"Wept … a good while" — this is the fifth time Joseph weeps.
Then Israel says, "Now let me die, since I have seen your face, that you are still alive."
A father who has waited twenty-two years, and the first sentence out of his mouth on seeing his son is, "Now let me die."

The last paragraph is intensely practical. Joseph coaches the family in how to answer Pharaoh — "that you shall say, 'Your servants have been keepers of livestock from our youth even until now, both we, and our fathers:' … that you may dwell in the land of Goshen; for every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians."
This is a very interesting arrangement. The Egyptians find shepherds abhorrent, and so shepherds get settled out on the edge, in the land of Goshen.

But that is precisely what Joseph wants. Living in Goshen, at some distance from Egypt's court, its temples and its culture, is the only way this family will not be assimilated out of existence over four hundred years.
Brothers and sisters, there are times when mainstream society shuts us out and we feel hard done by. But that "margin" is sometimes exactly the way God keeps hold of who we are.
Sometimes God uses other people's dislike to protect the set-apartness of his children.
Why is the one his father sends ahead to lead the way Judah, and not the firstborn?

Put the whole line together and it becomes very clear: in chapter 37 he proposed selling his brother; in chapter 38 he learned to admit he was wrong; in chapter 43 he stood surety for Benjamin; in chapter 44 he begged to be made a slave in his brother's place; and in chapter 46 his father sends him ahead to Joseph, to ask for someone to show the way. Reuben is the firstborn; Simeon and Levi are older; and yet the one the father sends is Judah. A person's place is something he walks into one step at a time — three chapters ago he was still the least likely candidate of them all. That is intensely practical for us today: you do not have to fight for a position. Shoulder what is yours to shoulder each time it comes round, and the position will find its own way to you.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
There are several places in this chapter you must be able to recognise.

The first distortion is preaching "sacrifice first, then decide" as a decision-making procedure. The point is not the ritual; it is a heart that is willing to hear a no. Preach it as a procedure and the congregation will go through the motions and then do exactly what they had meant to do all along. The test is this: has the congregation learned surrender, or learned a process?

The second distortion is preaching the descent into Egypt as God changing his mind. Back in chapter 15 God had told Abraham in advance: "Know for sure that your offspring will live as foreigners in a land that is not theirs, and will serve them. They will afflict them four hundred years." This is the plan, not a swerve. Preach it as a change of mind and your congregation will begin to doubt God's faithfulness.

The third distortion is skipping over the tension inside that number seventy. God promised offspring like the sand on the seashore, and at this moment there are seventy people. The text writes it down honestly. Skip over it, and the person whose present results are very small never learns to believe while things are still small.

The fourth distortion is turning "God goes down with you" into "so whatever you decide is fine". God said he would go down after Jacob had asked and had shown himself willing to obey. The promise of his presence is not an insurance policy for people who never asked at all.

The fifth distortion is preaching the settlement in Goshen as a rule that Christians ought to hide away and keep clear of society. Joseph himself is the prime minister, standing at the very centre of power; Goshen is how the family keeps its identity, not a regulation about sealing yourself off from the world. The measure of it is this: I am in the world, but I do not belong to the world.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: we are very good at finding spiritual-sounding language for decisions we have already made. Emigrating, changing jobs, buying a flat, a child's marriage — our minds were made up long ago, and then we say, "I did pray about it." Brothers and sisters, I am not saying those decisions were wrong. I am saying that was not asking. There is only one test of asking: if God says no, am I willing? This week, if you have a decision in front of you, put that one sentence to yourself first, and write the answer down. Once it is written down, you can no longer fool yourself.

The second question: we lose heart very easily over small numbers. The small group is down to three people. Sunday school has five children. You have served for ten years and there seems to be nothing you can see for it. And our culture is particularly given to comparing figures. The answer this chapter gives us is seventy — seventy people, in wagons, going down into a place they were afraid of. Four hundred years later, six hundred thousand came out. This week, do not lose heart because there are only seventy right now. Be faithful with the small patch in front of you; the numbers are God's business.
7. Living 321 Out — He Does Not Send Me In; He Comes In with Me
Brothers and sisters, let us bring this lesson back to the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. God said, "I will go down with you into Egypt," and the name of his Son is Immanuel — God with us. He does not merely send us; he came himself. He does not stand on the bank and shout; he went down into the water. My role model is this: he walks with people into the places they are most afraid of. So I too must walk with people, and not only pray for them.

The Bible is my standard. The standard is not "when the conditions are all right you may go". The standard is "Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don't lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight." Conditions will deceive you. The standard will not.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. God spoke to Jacob in the visions of the night. It is only when you go quiet that you can hear. The daytime is too noisy — too much information, too many people offering opinions. To rely on our intellect and on ourselves is to end up worried; you will simply go on calculating. To rely on the heart and on the Holy Spirit is to end up glad; he speaks in the moment when you are still.

Let Jesus be King. He had a hundred reasons to go straight there, and instead he stopped first and offered sacrifices. To let Jesus be King is to ask him first even when everything is at its most reasonable. If a person only asks God when he is in difficulty, then God is a consultant in his life, not a King.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. He offered sacrifices to "the God of his father, Isaac" — he acknowledged first that the source of all of this was not in himself, but in the God who made covenant with his fathers.

Establish God's system. Seventy people go down into Egypt, and four hundred years later what comes out is a nation. God begins a kingdom with one household. To establish God's system is to look not at this year's head count, but at that road four hundred years from now.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Vision in the Same Night
We are standing at Beersheba carrying four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "This is so obvious — does it really need asking?" Jacob had his son's invitation, Pharaoh's invitation, his whole family's expectation and the pressure of a famine. He asked anyway. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, reckoning that we are able to judge the matter ourselves; humility is returning to our originally intended position as human beings and asking first, even about the most obvious thing there is.

The fearful heart says, "If I take this step, I am afraid." The first sentence God gave him was "Don't be afraid", and the second was "I will go down with you." Brothers and sisters, God rarely takes the fear away. What he usually does is walk in and keep you company.

The ashamed heart says, "My family is in such a state — how could we possibly be fit to be God's nation?" Go and look at that list: a firstborn who forfeited his standing, two sons who died in Canaan, a daughter who was violated, a child born out of the most sordid episode in the family's past. God calls this crowd by name, one at a time, and takes them down with him. His list is not a roll of honour.

The wounded heart says, "This road that keeps going down — when does it come to an end?" God said, "I will also surely bring you up again" — and he used the emphatic construction, saying it twice over. On the road down, he has already spoken of the day of coming up.
Four kinds of heart, and one vision in the same night. And the God who calls people by name in the night is calling still today.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do
First, towards God. Appoint a Beersheba of your own — a fixed time and a fixed place, quiet before God. It need not be long; fifteen minutes will do. But it must be fixed.
Second, towards yourself. About the decision in your hands, ask one question: "If God says no, am I willing?" Write the answer down.
Third, towards people. Before you make a decision that affects your family, explain it to them properly first. Not an announcement — an explanation.
Fourth, towards daily living. If a decision comes up this week, sleep on it and pray about it before you answer. Do not say yes on the spot.
Fifth, towards the mission. Do not lose heart because there are only seventy people right now. Be faithful with the small patch in front of you, and see this week through.

Sixth, tell it to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First sentence: there is an old man of a hundred and thirty in the Bible who had to move to a place he was afraid of. Second sentence: what God said to him was, "I am going down there with you, and I will certainly bring you up again." Third sentence: the God I believe in is not the one who sends people in — he is the one who goes in with them.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that when everything is at its most reasonable, I will still ask God first.
I declare that when I ask, I am willing to accept a no.
I declare that when God says "go down", he has already said he will surely bring me up again.
I declare that I will not lose heart because there are only seventy people right now; God begins a nation with one household.
How do I tell whether I am really asking, or only after a spiritual-sounding way of putting it?

There is only one test: real asking means being willing to accept a no. A great deal of the time we say, "Let me pray about it," when in fact our minds are already made up and what we are after is a spiritual endorsement. So before you pray, put one question to yourself: if God says no, will I not go? If the answer is that you will go anyway, then be honest and call it a decision; do not dress it up as guidance. In practice you can add two further safeguards: write your reasons down and show them to someone who will not simply agree with you; and set a definite deadline and a definite exit condition — a person willing to set an exit condition is usually a person who is genuinely asking.

An old man, with his whole household, his livestock and a lifetime's belongings, stands in front of the altar at Beersheba. Ahead of him is Egypt — the place his own father was stopped from entering by God. Behind him is Canaan, the land he has walked all his life.
That night God called him by name and said: I am going too.

So the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on other people, not on our circumstances. Not I, but Christ. Because the God who said, "I will go down with you into Egypt," afterwards went down himself into a place far deeper — he became flesh and lived among us, and he was called Immanuel; he went down into death and came up again out of death, and he said, "I will come again and will receive you to myself; that where I am, you may be there also."

May God bless every one of us: that before we take a large step we would go round by the altar first; that on the road that goes downwards we would remember the other half of the same sentence he spoke; and that we would not think little of the day of seventy people, because God is beginning a nation in the middle of it. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point of this lesson into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be taken home to finish.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ Real asking means being willing to accept a no. That decision you made recently — were you praying for guidance, or for an endorsement?
2. ★★ "I will go down with you into Egypt." He does not send us in; he comes in with us. How does that sentence apply to the difficulty in front of you now?
3. ★ When God says "go down", the same sentence has already said he will surely bring you up again. What does that say to the stretch of road you are currently going down?
4. ★★ Seventy people are the starting point of "the sand on the seashore". What does that say to the discouragement of "there are too few of us"?

Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it out loud, not that they answer beautifully. If someone speaks in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (the conditions are all right, so what is there to ask?), fearful (I do not dare walk into that situation), ashamed (does a name like mine belong on that list?), wounded (what I do is so small that nobody cares). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "I will go down with you into Egypt. I will also surely bring you up again." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ What is the decision you have in hand right now? If God says no, can you let it go?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The place I least want to walk into is …"
9. ★★ This week, on which day and in what place will you "go round by Beersheba" — making one special trip of prayer for that decision?

Leader's reminder: the question about the decision in someone's hands may touch a major choice of life — work, moving abroad, marriage, medical treatment. Do not make anyone's decision for him, and do not say, "Just go in faith and it will be fine." Help him set out clearly the people he ought to ask and the things he ought to check.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, which decision is one the whole family ought to pray about together? Say how you are going to open the conversation.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or in your service, which thing do you "already know to do without asking"? Do you really not need to ask?

12. ★★★ The practice of the seventy: this week, say the names of the few people you are responsible for out loud in prayer, one at a time, instead of counting how many there are. Say when you are going to do it.

13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him the decision you are wavering over, and ask him to put this question to you: "And what if God says no?" Say his name here and now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First sentence: there is an old man of a hundred and thirty in the Bible who was moving his whole household to a foreign country, and although every condition was right, he took a detour first in order to pray. Second sentence: that night God said to him, "I will go down with you, and I will also surely bring you up again." Third sentence: so I believe that God does not send us into our troubles — he comes into them with us. Write down here and now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the decision you are wavering over, and the day you are setting aside specially to pray. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to make us willing to ask even when all the conditions are right, and to make us remember, on the road that goes downwards, the second half of the sentence he has already spoken.
